pipeline.d: 1,951 pages of the Breaking Bad fan wiki (CC BY-SA) via its API: episodes, characters, places, objects.
qwen3:14b reads each page and writes 9,698 grounded Q&A pairs: a plain answer plus the same answer in Saul's voice.
Every question comes in 3–4 wordings, because small models memorize a fact only when they see it said differently several times.
29,433 training rows. Full fine-tune of 30M / 135M / 0.6B students on one RTX 4070 Ti, plus refusal rows for drug & weapon recipes.
Exported to GGUF (Q8 / Q5) and served as static files. llama.cpp compiled to WebAssembly (wllama) runs them in this tab.

how: Why distill? A 14B model with web search is slow (tens of seconds per answer), needs a GPU and the internet, and costs money per query. For a narrow domain you can move that knowledge into a model 100× smaller that answers in a second on a phone, with no server at all.

Sequence-level distillation. The student never sees the wiki. It only sees what the teacher wrote, so everything it knows came through the teacher. Ollama returns text, not probabilities, so this is the same "learn from the teacher's answers" recipe used to make most small open models. Part two shows what changes when an API also leaks probabilities.

Why the student can beat the teacher. Without search, qwen3:14b half-remembers the show from pre-training and confidently invents details ("the car wash is called Lucky 7"). The student was trained only on the teacher's grounded answers, so on this narrow topic it is more accurate than the teacher's own memory. Outside the topic it knows nothing, by design.

Honest numbers. The 100 fan questions were written by hand before training and checked against the wiki. Held-out rephrasings are wordings of trained facts that were removed from training. Answers are graded by keyword for the fan set and by the teacher (with the wiki answer as reference) for the rest. Everything (1,951 pages, 9,698 facts, 29,433 rows) was produced on one Windows PC with an RTX 4070 Ti; code is on GitHub.

cards.title: Hide the logprobs
cards.what: Many APIs return the probability of every candidate token (logprobs). That is a gift to a thief: instead of one answer per question, the student learns the teacher's whole belief at every word. This is classic Hinton-style soft-label distillation.
cards.how: Attacker: Qwen3-0.6B (same tokenizer as the teacher), the same 1,500 harvested facts, trained once on text only and once with top-20 logprobs (KL loss).

cards.result: with logprobs 60% vs text only 66%. Hiding logprobs costs honest users nothing. Here it did not help: with short one-fact answers and only top-20 logprobs, matching the teacher's distribution was a worse target than just copying its words. Logprobs pay off on long, open-ended outputs and with full vocabularies.

cards.title: Rate limits & query budgets
cards.what: A student only knows what it was shown. Per-account, per-IP and per-device limits (device fingerprinting, as in my LeakCheck page) cap how much a thief can harvest before paying a lot or getting noticed.
cards.how: The same attacker trained on the first 100 / 300 / 700 / 1,500 facts it managed to harvest.
cards.result: accuracy tracks the budget almost linearly, so whoever controls the budget controls the copy.

cards.title: Extraction detection
cards.what: Thieves don't ask like fans. Fans ask about Walt, Jesse and Saul and come back to favorites; a harvester systematically walks the long tail (every minor character, every location) because it needs coverage.
cards.how: Logistic regression over a sliding window of 20 queries: distinct-page ratio, long-tail share, timing. Tested on 300 simulated sessions of each kind (simulated traffic, not real users).

cards.title: Antidistillation sampling
cards.what: Change how the teacher picks words: among the words the teacher itself finds good, prefer the ones a typical student finds hardest to learn. The answer stays right for people but becomes a worse training signal. Simplified version of Savani et al. 2025.
cards.how: Inside the teacher's top-p 0.9 nucleus, re-rank tokens by teacher log-prob − λ·(proxy student log-prob), λ = 1, with Qwen3-0.6B as proxy.
